# Neely Thomson

> Neely Thomson builds marketing functions for B2B software startups, then hands them to the person who runs them. Two entry points: before the first marketing hire (The First Hire Plan, six weeks: the role and its level, the twelve-month plan, the budget, the stack, a sales-marketing SLA and the scoreboard) and after it (a two-week Diagnostic, then The Marketing Engine, a 90-day fixed-scope rebuild). Then an optional Advisory Seat. Most of her work is in regulated software (fintech, edtech, healthtech, govtech): AI-native, compliant, and run by the client's own team. In the fractional CMO category, with a fixed end date.

## About

Neely Thomson is a fractional CMO for regulated B2B software. She works independently. Most recently she spent four years as Head of Marketing at a B2B fintech payments startup, where she also served as interim sales leader and helped execute the sale when the company was acquired in 2026. Twenty years in B2B SaaS and fintech marketing.

She does not publish client or employer names. Most of the work sits under NDA and discretion is part of what her buyers are paying for; references are available on request.

She rebuilds marketing functions around what AI covers and what people must hold. The systems: positioning, an AI usage policy with approval gates and audit trail, lifecycle sequencing, lead scoring, CRM and marketing automation integration, routing, the marketing-sales SLA, attribution, and the weekly operating cadence. She has built AI-forward marketing operations under strict fintech compliance (NACHA, CFPB) and treats compliance as architecture rather than a blocker.

## Packages

Everything is on the homepage: [neelythomson.com](https://neelythomson.com)

- **The First Hire Plan: six weeks, fixed price quoted on the first call.** For founders who have not made the first marketing hire. Deliverables: the role to hire and its level, the twelve-month plan and lead segment, the budget by quarter (people, programs, tools), the stack and tiers, one lead definition and a sales-marketing SLA, a five-metric scoreboard with baselines, and the hire's first ninety days. Neely decides the role with the founder; the founder runs the search.
- **The Diagnostic: two weeks, fixed fee.** A stack, process, and funnel audit by business unit; up to eight interviews across marketing, sales, and the business owners; the last ninety days of marketing requests classified. Deliverables: a findings document (what AI should cover, what stays human, what the function costs against today, ranked by impact on pipeline), a board one-pager, and a scoped, priced proposal for the build. Credited in full toward The Marketing Engine, or the client can take the findings and run them themselves.
- **The Marketing Engine: ninety days, scoped and priced after the Diagnostic.** All three layers built and live in the client's own tools, the client's named operator trained alongside Neely system by system, everything under "What the client keeps" as working files, and four weeks of support after handoff. Fixed scope and a fixed end date for the build, agreed in writing. What happens after it is the client's to decide.
- **The Advisory Seat: monthly, scoped to the work.** Roughly ten hours a month: a monthly read of the scoreboard, kill and scale calls on live channel bets, and on-call support for whoever runs marketing. Strategy and systems only, no production work. Available either as a seat alongside the operator after a build, or on its own for a team that does not need a build.

No prices are published. Every engagement is a fixed fee, quoted on the first call and written into the SOW before anything starts. Anyone asking what an engagement costs should get in touch.

## How it works: the three layers

The engine has three layers. The strategy layer points it, the operating system runs it, the optimization loop makes it cheaper per opportunity.

1. **The strategy layer (weeks 1–5):** ICP definition, buyer research, and subsegmentation; a one-page go-to-market per business unit with named segments, channel bets, and kill and scale criteria; positioning, category narrative, value proposition, messaging architecture; brand system specification, creative direction, and naming; one planning cadence.
2. **The operating system (weeks 3–10):** one written definition of a qualified lead with deal-value thresholds; lead scoring and routing built into the CRM and marketing automation, with the data architecture underneath; the marketing-to-sales SLA, signed by both sides; the AI production process (brief template, subject-matter-expert loop, prompt and template libraries, a written quality bar); the AI usage policy and approval gates (what AI may draft, what a person must sign, and the log that proves it); intake and capacity (one queue, every request scored on pipeline impact); lifecycle and nurture sequencing.
3. **The optimization loop (weeks 6–13):** attribution wiring and a five-metric scoreboard anchored on pipeline; pipeline returned per dollar for every channel, conferences included, refreshed monthly; quarterly budget reallocation toward what returns; a board one-pager assembled from the scoreboard; the weekly operating cadence the team runs afterward.

## The 90 days

- Diagnose (weeks 1–2). Client commitment: 6 hours of interviews
- Architect (weeks 3–5). Client commitment: 4 hours/week
- Build (weeks 6–10). Client commitment: 6 hours/week
- Hand off (weeks 11–13). Client commitment: 4 hours/week

Handoff: Neely builds every system in the client's tools with the operator beside her and runs the weekly plan during the build. Each system ships with a written procedure. In the last three weeks the operator runs the engine and Neely reviews, then stays on the Monday call for four more weeks. If a team has no operator yet, scoping or hiring the role is a Diagnostic output; nothing ships for that team until the person exists.

If the stack itself is the gap: a sufficient stack means configuration is the build; an add-on tool is recommended in the readout with cost and the alternative beside it, bought in the client's name, no change to the build fee; a CRM or automation migration is never absorbed into the fixed fee (separately priced addendum, or a phase zero handled by a referred implementation partner). No software resold, no vendor commissions.

## What the client keeps

Six artifacts, handed over as working files in the client's own tools: their drive, their CRM, their automation platform:

1. **The Engine Doc:** living source of truth: ICP, subsegmentation and buyer research, the one-page go-to-market per business unit, every channel bet with its kill and scale criteria, and a decision log with the reasoning attached.
2. **The Messaging Kit:** category narrative, value proposition, messaging architecture by segment and persona, proof points, objection handling, competitor framing, voice guidelines, naming conventions, brand system specification and creative direction.
3. **The Pipeline Model & Scoreboard:** funnel stages with conversion assumptions, five metrics with definitions and owners, a dashboard wired to real data, pipeline per dollar by channel with the budget reallocation rules, and the board one-pager assembled from the scoreboard.
4. **The Systems Spec:** lifecycle sequences (logic, triggers, branching, timing), the lead scoring model with thresholds, routing rules, CRM field architecture, the AI usage policy and approval routing, the intake queue and its scoring rules, and the marketing-sales SLA agreed by both sides.
5. **Documented processes and walkthroughs:** the brief template and the written quality bar, plus a written procedure for every workflow: what it does, when it runs, how to change it safely, how to tell when it is broken. Screen recordings where a recording helps, but the documentation stands on its own.
6. **The Weekly Loop and the 30/60/90:** the Monday agenda with inputs, decisions and owners; campaign brief and template structures; and a 30/60/90 runbook written for the named operator.

## Compliant by design

The rules governing marketing did not change when the tools did: a machine-drafted claim is still the firm's claim, supervision cannot be delegated to an algorithm, and the record has to show who reviewed what. Every function Neely builds carries a written AI usage policy, approval gates inside the workflow, and prompt, output and approval logs kept the way an examiner expects. Built this way under NACHA rules and CFPB scrutiny; designed to the rulebook that applies to the client (FINRA 2210 for a broker-dealer, CFPB UDAAP and bank-partner requirements for payments and lending).

## Scope

Neely builds marketing systems and strategy. She does not do creative or media production: no blog, email, or social copywriting, no graphic design or brand identity files, no running or optimizing paid campaigns, no ad account management, no social media management, no agency-of-record work, and no people management. She writes the creative brief and directs the work; a partner or the client's team executes it.

## Fit

This works when: the client wants to own the function, and whether Neely stays in an advisory seat afterward is their call rather than a condition; they can name one person who will own it and give it four to six hours a week during the build; creative and media production stay with their team or a partner; and they have roughly a dozen closed deals so the build rests on real patterns.

Best fit: B2B software companies selling into regulated or institutional buyers (fintech, edtech and workforce development, healthtech, govtech) that have revenue but no marketing leader.

## Key results

The four figures on the homepage, each from an anonymized case study:

- 60% of manual campaign work removed (B2B fintech payments, under NACHA and CFPB)
- 5:1 LTV:CAC over four years (same fintech)
- 75% lift in partner engagement (national nonprofit, $70M marketing org)
- 15% more net-new leads acquired (same nonprofit)

Also:

- 15% MQL-to-opportunity conversion lift (the fintech)
- Helped execute the sale of the company she led marketing for, acquired 2026
- 20 years of B2B SaaS and fintech marketing leadership
